# Revisiting the trends in global inequality

## Abstract

I analyze trends in global income distribution since 1950 using a new companion WIID dataset with standardized country income percentiles. I investigate the robustness of these trends with respect to key data choices, as well as the degree to which the inequality trend depends on specific distributional views (such as the use of absolute versus relative inequality, or relative emphasis at the bottom versus the top). The results show a robust increase in absolute inequality, along with a more nuanced trend in relative inequality, with a very robust decline after 2000 that was interrupted by the COVID crisis but is expected to continue at least until 2028.

## Introduction

From a global perspective, social well-being increases with the average standard of living, as well as with greater equality in its distribution among all citizens of the world, regardless of where they live. 1 There is no doubt that average living standards have increased unprecedentedly over the past few decades, not only in terms of income but also in other dimensions. This has contributed enormously to reducing absolute poverty levels. However, the question of whether they have also made the world more equal is more complicated. The relationship between inequality and growth is complex and the empirical evidence is mixed; while some types of growth can increase inequality, others can be more inclusive. 2 The literature on global inequality has since the early 2000 s provided some mixed and fragmented results 3 due to the lack of appropriate data and the use of different, sometimes contradictory, approaches. 4 his paper aims to contribute to this growing literature in different ways. First, I present a new dataset with annual information on income percentile distributions by country (also aggregated at the global level) from 1950 to 2020, with projections until 2028. This new dataset complements the World Income Inequality Database (WIID), the successor to Deininger and Squire's (1996) initial compilation. 5 econd, I use this new dataset to revisit global trends in inequality using a broad approach to fully describe distributional changes at different points in the distribution. Furthermore, rather than imposing particular views on inequality, I assess the level of consensus between different approaches, concerning how inequality changes in the context of economic growth (relative versus absolute views of inequality) as well as the level of consensus between various distributive sensitivities (and measures) that put more emphasis on changes that occur in different parts of the global distribution (for example, whether we give more weight to lower income growth at the bottom or greater concentration of income at the top as the main source of inequality). I also analyze the sensitivity of global inequality trends to the use of alternative measures of countries' per capita income from different data sources, as well as to correcting survey-based estimates for possible underestimation of top incomes within countries.

Third, the paper uses an innovative approach based on the Recentered Influence Function (RIF) (Gradín, 2020b) to quantify the contribution of major countries and regions to changes in total inequality over time. Following an expanded Blinder-Oaxaca approach, these contributions are consistently decomposed into contributions (ceteris paribus) to changes in inequality between countries, inequality within countries, and a composition effect (due to differential population growth) that add up to the total change observed over a period. 6 he results of the paper are very consistent with previous evidence based on survey data but allow for a more detailed, systematic, and comprehensive analysis of the patterns in global distributional trends in terms of time and geographic coverage, as well as the distributional approaches that can be used. These results are also reconciled with those based on alternative measures of per capita income across countries, or on correcting for the underestimation of top incomes in survey data.

In summary, the results show unambiguously that absolute inequality, which requires greater increases in constant dollars among the poorest people over time for inequality to decline in a context of economic growth, has increased continuously since 1950, apart from brief episodes around major global economic recessions (in which dollar income losses tend to be greater for the rich). This increase has affected both the between-and within-country components, which reinforce each other. However, a more complex and different story emerges in terms of relative inequality, which only requires higher growth rates (not dollar amounts) in the lower percentiles for inequality to decline. This is reflected in the lack of complete unanimity in the direction of inequality, especially in the 1980 s and 1990 s, added to the results being sensitive to key data choices. There is a greater level of consensus and robustness that relative inequality has decreased since 2000 (unless there is extreme sensitivity towards the world's very rich or very poor). This fall in inequality was driven by China, India, and other countries catching up with the rest, only partially offset by heterogeneous trends in inequality within countries and faster population growth in sub-Saharan Africa, the poorest and most unequal region. This decline is expected to continue at least until 2028.

## Data

The analysis of global inequality faces considerable data limitations due to a lack of sufficient information collected consistently over time and across countries. To address this, I have put together a new dataset on global inequality (UNU-WIDER 2022a) that is based on a classic database for the analysis of inequality across countries: the WIID (see UNU-WIDER 2022b). The WIID was first launched in 2000, continuing one of the most successful early initiatives, by Deininger and Squire (1996), to collect cross-country information on inequality. The WIID, which has more than 20,000 data points, collects and stores information on income inequality for almost every country in the world (197 countries or territories and four historical entities) over the longest possible period for which reliable data are available. Information is now primarily obtained from a variety of public sources. The dataset is a unique combination of data from the most prominent current data 2 The literature has investigated the impact of different types of structural transformation on inequality, as well as the impact of inequality on growth. Regarding the latter, for example, Baymul and Sen (2022) found that in contrast to the Kuznets hypothesis, the movement of workers to manufacturing unambiguously decreases income inequality, irrespective of the stage of structural transformation that a particular country is in. In the case of services-driven structural transformation, inequality does follow an inverted U-shaped curve, but with heterogeneity across countries. On the other hand, a recent review by Baselgia & Foellmi, 2022 showed that empirical estimates on the overall impact of inequality on economic growth remain inconclusive, with both significant positive and negative effects found depending on the specification. They did find more evidence for a negative link than for a positive one among developing countries.

3 From a long-term perspective, combining historical series with survey data from the most recent decades, global inequality had an upward trend until 1980, followed first by stagnation between 1980 and 1990, and then by a decline (Bourguignon and Morrisson, 2002, and Bourguignon, 2015,2019). Anand and Segal (2008) reviewed early estimates of global inequality based on household surveys, pointing to an increase in inequality before 1970 or 1980, along with declines between 1990 and 2000, but with mixed evidence about what happened between 1980 and 1990 or 1995. The more recent decline in global inequality is also consistent with other findings, such as the analysis by Lakner and Milanovic (2016) for 1988-2008, expanded by Milanovic (2022) for 2008-13, as well as by Niño-Zarazúa et al. (2017) for 1970-2010, or Davies and Shorrocks (2021) for 2010-15, among others. 4 Most previous analyses describing inequality in recent decades have been conducted using the Gini index as the primary measure and using survey data, although other indices and approaches have increasingly been used with different distributional implications that can alter the conclusions on the trend of inequality in certain periods. This can be clearly seen in the stream of literature that, after combining survey data with tax records and national accounts, moved the focus of inequality analysis to the evolution of income concentration at the top of the distribution (e.g., example, World Inequality Lab 2018, 2022a, Chancel & Piketty, 2021 and related research). This literature more clearly emphasizes a higher level of inequality, especially the concentration of income accrued by the richest people. Even stronger implications can be found when the focus shifts from a relative to an absolute view of inequality (as, for example, in Ravallion, 2004,2018,2021 and Niño-Zarazúa et al., 2017), since differences in income among people measured in constant international dollars (absolute view) have generally increased over time, even when growth rates were strongest among the poor (relative view). 5 The WIID and Deininger and Squire's (1996) compilation have been widely used in this literature, including early studies such as Chotikapanich et al. (1997), Dowrick and Akmal (2005) of quantifying a country's contribution by assessing the change in inequality after removing it from the sample. The approach used here ensures that the sum of the contributions of all countries or group of countries adds up to the total change in inequality and does not depend on the order in which countries are considered or how they are grouped.

First, it is necessary to select the observations to use, because in many cases there may be more than one distribution per country and year (for example, from different sources or referring to different resource measures). Second, we must address this heterogeneity in the concepts of well-being measured, geographic coverage, and sources. Although the most common concept of well-being refers to some type of definition of income expressed in per capita terms, a substantial number of observations in Africa and Asia refer to per capita consumption. Some observations may refer to income per household or equivalent adult. Similarly, income can be gross or net (after taxes and social contributions have been deducted). Most observations refer to the national level and some refer to urban areas or exclude specific parts of a country. Furthermore, the values reported by different sources may diverge in other methodological aspects, such as the survey or the treatment of non-response, etc. Third, only observations that report income shares will be used.
